full_judgment:
Md. Altaf Hossain, J: In this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, an order dated 25.8.81 passed by the Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 385 of 1978 dismissing the appeal all merits is under challenged. 

 2. The opposite party No.1 Sultan Ahmed Khan as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 11 6 of 1974 on 13.9.74 in the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong against the petitioner defendant No. 1 and opposite parties 2 and 3 pro-forma respondents defendant for specific performance of contract sale and other reliefs. The suit was decreed ex-parte on 30.7.75. The petitioner filed an application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code on 30.8.75 which was registered as Miscellaneous case No. 75 of 1975 for restoration of the suit The Miscellaneous case was dismissed for default on 26 8.78. The petitioner thereupon preferred an appeal to the District Judge, Chittagong which was registered as Miscellaneous Appeal No. 385 of 1978. This appeal was dismissed on merits on 25.8.81 by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong to whom the appeal was transferred. Being aggrieved, the defendant petitioner has moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

 Sub-rule (1) of rule 17 authorises a dismissal of the appeal on the ground of non- appearance of the appellant when the appeal is called on for hearing, It seems evident that sub-rule (1) of rule 17 does not authorise the Court to go into the merits of the appeal and to give decision on merits. A power to go into the merits of the case would necessarily include a power either to allow the appeal or to dismiss the appeal. It is not conceivable that when the Court has power to examine the merits of the appeal, it does not have the power to allow the appeal even if the merits so demand. The only power that is given under sub-rule (1) is a power of dismissal. It necessarily follows that under this sub-rule the Court has no power to go into the merits and dismiss an appeal on merits. The view that an order of dismissal of an appeal on merits under sub-rule (1) of rule 17 is illegal finds support in a number of decisions. In the case of Taher Sheikh Chowkidar and others Vs. Otaruddi Howlader and miters reported in A.l.R. 1929 Cal. 475 a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court held that under Order 41, rule 17 the Court is not authorised to consider an appeal in the absence of the appellant and decide it on merits. In the case of Digendra Chandra Pal vs. Radha Bellav Pal reported in A.I R. 1953 Assam 191 the High Court of Assam held that the court has no power  to proceed to decide the appeal on merits in the absence of the appellant or his Counsel. It can dismiss the appeal by reason of absence of the appellant. In the case of Kundha Singh V.s. The Punjab State and others reported in A.I.R. 1962 Punjab 82 of the Court held after considering a good number of decisions in some of which a contrary view was also expressed, that the appellate court had no jurisdiction to dismiss he appeal on merits under Order 41, rule 17 and its order should be treated as an order of dismissed for default and the remedy of the aggrieved party to move an application under Order 41, rule 19 CPC  will remain open. In the case of Masafir Mghton Vs. Mt. Bachani reported in A.l.R 1963 Patna 1 a Division Bench of Patna High Court has held that the appellate court has no Jurisdiction to hear the appeal on merits where the appellant does not appear at the time the appeal is called on for hearing. The only course open to the appellate court in the circumstances is to adjourn the case to another date, or to make an order dismissing the appeal ex parte. In the case of Deo Dutta Singh and others vs. Ram Naresh Singh and others reported in AIR. 1973 Patna 166 a Division Bench of Patna High Court has held that when the appellant does not appear when the appeal is called on for hearing the court may either adjourn it or dismiss it for default but it has no power to dismiss the appeal on merits. In respectful agreement with the view expressed in the above decision. I also hold that when the appellant or his counsel fails to appear when an appeal is called on for hearing the appellate court can only dismiss the appeal for default or may adjourn it. It has no power to deliver judgment of the appeal on merits. Even if the appeal is dismissed on merits this will be treated as a dismissal for default under Order 41, rule 17 and the appellant's remedy under rule 19 of that order will remain open. 

 4. Mr. Mokbul Ahmed the learned Advocate for the opposite parties, however, submits that the jurisdiction nude section 115(1) C.P.C. as it read at the relevant time, can be exercised by this court only on the ground of an error of law apparent on the face of the record in the decision. In the instant case the records show that the learned Advocate for the appellant appeared before the appellate court and the appeal has been dismissed on merits. The learned Advocate also submits that the contention of the petitioner that the learned Advocate for the appellant did not appear when suit was called on for hearing is not borne out by record. It is also denied on the side of the opposite parties, It could not be disputed by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that whether the learned Advocate for the appellant had appeared when the appeal was called on for hearing has become a disputed question of fact. This Court in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction shall not enter into a disputed question of face and shall go by the record and shall not give relief if the learned Advocate for the petitioner fails to show any error apparent on the face of the record that is to say, if from the record the learned Advocate fails to show that the appeal was dismissed on merits in spite of the absence of the learned Advocate for the appellant. In the instant case the judgment itself records the presence of Mr . Md. Khairul Islam. Advocate for the appellant. Order dated 21.8.81 of the appellant Court appearing from the record of the appellate court reads as follows: 

 5. Therefore, from the records it appears that parties appeared when the appeal was called on for hearing, Mr. C.R. Das, the learned Advocate submits that the noting of the name of Mr. Kharul Islam in the, judgment of the appellate Court and noting of appearance of the parties in the order dated 21.8.81 are contrary to facts. I have already observed that in the exercise of revisional jurisdiction the court will only go by records and the facts appearing from the records. If the allegation of the petitioner that when the appeal was called on for hearing the learned Advocate for the appellant could not appear is true the appellant  may seek his remedy under Order 41, rule 19 C.P.C. where this disputed question of fact can be investigated and decided. To conclude I hold and find that no case of error of law apparent on the face of the record in the decision has been made out so as to attract the revisional jurisdiction of this court.
